written.q: Explain Conway's Law and how it relates to microservices.
written.a: Organisations that design systems produce designs that copy their communication structures: boundaries appear where communication is weakest (separate UI, backend and DB teams give separate UI, backend and database pieces). Cross-functional teams that own business capabilities (ordering, payments) naturally produce independently owned services, so microservices follow from capability-owning teams and are not a cure for silos.

written.q: Describe the controller, service and repository layers and trace a registration request through them.
written.a: Controller: receives HTTP, validates input, returns status codes. Service: business rules (a student cannot join a full course). Repository: reads and writes the database, the only place with SQL. Request: browser POST /courses/42/registrations, routed to the controller, which calls the service; the service checks the course is not full; the repository inserts a row; the service returns the registration; the controller replies 201 Created with JSON. The rule lives in one place and works for any client.

written.q: Compare monolith, modular monolith and microservices and give the decision checklist for choosing microservices.
written.a: Monolith: one deployable unit, simple to build and debug, one-DB transactions, but everything scales and deploys together. Modular monolith: one deployment with clean internal boundaries (best for small teams). Microservices: independently deployed capability services with their own data and team, giving independent deploys, scaling and failure isolation at the cost of network complexity, eventual consistency and operations. Need them when several teams block releases, one part needs 10x scaling or different tech, you can run 24/7 ops and boundaries are stable; avoid them with one small team, a changing domain, no ops or no users yet.

written.q: List the costs of microservices and five patterns used when splitting.
written.a: Costs: network failures, no shared transaction (eventual consistency), operational weight (pipelines, monitoring, discovery), permanent boundaries; challenges include debugging across services, testing, API versioning and local development. Patterns: API gateway, database per service, service discovery, circuit breaker, asynchronous messaging.

written.q: When should communication be synchronous and when asynchronous? Contrast orchestration and choreography.
written.a: Synchronous (REST/gRPC) when the caller needs the answer now (authorise a payment). Asynchronous (events via a broker) when nobody is waiting (email receipts, notifications, analytics). Orchestration uses a central conductor, giving a visible flow and clear error handling but coupling to everyone (use for money and critical workflows); choreography has services react to events, giving loose coupling but a hidden flow and scattered errors (use for broadcasts).
